```{python}
#| label: setup
import json
from fractions import Fraction

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

from acme_eval.claims import claim

metrics = pd.read_csv("outputs/metrics.csv")
segments = pd.read_csv("outputs/segments.csv")
calibration = pd.read_csv("outputs/calibration.csv")
curves = pd.read_csv("outputs/curves.csv")
summary = json.loads(open("outputs/summary.json").read())

value = metrics.pivot(index="metric", columns="version", values="value")
low = metrics.pivot(index="metric", columns="version", values="low")
high = metrics.pivot(index="metric", columns="version", values="high")
auc = value.loc["roc_auc"]
best = summary["best_version"]
claim(best == auc.idxmax(), "The release called best has the highest ROC AUC.")
rival = auc.drop(best).idxmax()  # the runner-up, compared with the best on slide 3
first = auc.index[0]             # the first release, as a reference on the ROC slide
releases = pd.DataFrame(summary["releases"]).set_index("version")
calls = summary["calls_made"]
top_share = summary["top_share"]

# The figures use the report's colour-blind-safe palette (Okabe-Ito) and acme.scss's ink and paper.
colors = {"v1": "#999999", "v2": "#0072B2", "v3": "#D55E00"}
INK, PAPER = "#1b2733", "#fbfaf7"
plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.size": 15, "axes.labelsize": 15, "legend.fontsize": 14,
    "text.color": INK, "axes.labelcolor": INK, "axes.edgecolor": INK,
    "xtick.color": INK, "ytick.color": INK,
    "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False,
    "figure.facecolor": "none", "axes.facecolor": "none",  # the slide shows through
})


def percent(share: float, digits: int = 1) -> str:
    """A share between 0 and 1, as a percentage."""
    return f"{100 * share:.{digits}f}%"


def fraction_words(share: float) -> str:
    """A share such as 0.1 in words ("a tenth"), for a title."""
    words = {2: "half", 3: "a third", 4: "a quarter", 5: "a fifth", 10: "a tenth"}
    fraction = Fraction(share).limit_denominator(100)
    claim(fraction.numerator == 1 and fraction.denominator in words,
          "The called share can be said in words as a simple fraction.")
    return words[fraction.denominator]
```

::: {.notes}
Acme Signals is a fictional two-person company; the bank data are real (UCI Bank Marketing).
Every number on these slides is read from outputs/, which scripts/evaluate.py writes once.
The full evidence is in the evaluation report and the model card. The question for today:
which release the call centre should use for the next campaign, and on what conditions.
:::

## `{python} best` reaches `{python} percent(value.loc["recall_top10", best])` of subscribers by calling `{python} fraction_words(top_share)` of the list {#headline}

```{python}
#| label: headline
claim(value.loc["lift_top10", best] > 1, "The best release finds more subscribers per call than random calls.")
```

- [`{python} f"{calls:,}"`]{.stat} calls: the top `{python} percent(top_share, 0)` of the
  `{python} f"{summary['test_rows']:,}"` test contacts
- [`{python} percent(value.loc["recall_top10", best])`]{.stat} of all their subscribers
  are among them
- [`{python} f"{value.loc['lift_top10', best]:.1f}"`×]{.stat} the subscribers per call of
  calling at random

::: {.notes}
The call centre calls the top `{python} percent(top_share, 0)` of the ranked list, so the
business metric is recall in that top share: of all subscribers in the test set, the share
the calls reach. For `{python} best` it is
`{python} percent(value.loc["recall_top10", best])`, with a `{python} percent(summary["confidence"], 0)` bootstrap interval of
`{python} percent(low.loc["recall_top10", best])` to
`{python} percent(high.loc["recall_top10", best])`. Calling at random would reach about
`{python} percent(top_share, 0)` of them. The base rate is
`{python} percent(summary["base_rate"])`: about one contact in
`{python} f"{1 / summary['base_rate']:.0f}"` subscribes. Lift is the called contacts'
subscription rate over the base rate. The test set is a held-out
`{python} percent(summary["test_size"], 0)` of the data, never used in training.
:::

```{python}
#| label: compare-setup
shown = {
    "roc_auc": ("ROC AUC", True, "{:.3f}"),
    "average_precision": ("Average precision", True, "{:.3f}"),
    "brier": ("Brier score, lower is better", False, "{:.3f}"),
    "recall_top10": (f"Recall, top {percent(top_share, 0)}", True, None),
    "lift_top10": (f"Lift, top {percent(top_share, 0)}", True, "{:.2f}"),
}
# Strictly better: a tie is not a win, whichever way the metric points.
better = {m: (value.loc[m, best] > value.loc[m, rival]) if higher
          else (value.loc[m, best] < value.loc[m, rival])
          for m, (_, higher, _) in shown.items()}
claim(all(better.values()), "The best release beats the runner-up on every metric shown.")
models = {"logistic_regression": "Logistic regression", "gradient_boosting": "Gradient boosting"}


def release_column(version: str) -> None:
    """Print one release's column: what it is, then its metrics, the better value in bold."""
    release = releases.loc[version]
    print(f"### {version} · released {release['month']}\n")
    print(f"{release['description']}\n")
    def shown_as(metric: str, number: float) -> str:
        form = shown[metric][2]
        return percent(number) if form is None else form.format(number)

    for metric, (label, higher, form) in shown.items():
        text = shown_as(metric, value.loc[metric, version])
        texts = {v: shown_as(metric, value.loc[metric, v]) for v in (best, rival)}
        winner = best if better[metric] else rival
        # Bold the better value only when the difference shows at the precision printed.
        bold = version == winner and texts[best] != texts[rival]
        print(f"- {label}: {f'**{text}**' if bold else text}")
```

## `{python} best` beats `{python} rival` on all `{python} len(shown)` metrics, with the same `{python} f"{calls:,}"` calls {#compare}

```{python}
release_column(rival)
```

::: {.notes}
Both releases see every field known before the call; `{python} best` swaps logistic
regression for gradient-boosted trees, which can find interactions between fields.
The better value of each metric is in bold. ROC AUC and average precision summarise the
whole ranking; the Brier score checks the probabilities; recall and lift are for the
`{python} f"{calls:,}"` contacts that are called. All are computed on the same test
contacts, and the intervals come from the same bootstrap resamples (see the caveats).
:::

## `{python} best` ranks the whole list best: ROC AUC `{python} f"{auc[best]:.3f}"`, against `{python} f"{auc[first]:.3f}"` for `{python} first` {#roc}

```{python}
#| label: roc-figure
#| fig-cap: "ROC curves on the test contacts. The dashed diagonal is a random ranking."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of true-positive rate against false-positive rate, one curve per release. Every curve rises above the dashed diagonal of a random ranking; the best release's curve encloses the most area and the first release's the least."
claim((auc > 0.5).all(), "Every curve rises above the diagonal (alt text).")
claim(auc.idxmin() == first, "The first release's curve is the lowest (title and alt text).")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.2))
for version, points in curves[curves["curve"] == "roc"].groupby("version"):
    ax.plot(points["x"], points["y"], color=colors[version], linewidth=2.5,
            label=f"{version}: ROC AUC {auc[version]:.3f}")
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], linestyle="--", color="#555555", linewidth=1)
ax.set_xlabel("False-positive rate")
ax.set_ylabel("True-positive rate")
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.05, 0.5))
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
A ROC curve follows the ranking from the top of the list down. The further a curve bows
towards the top left, the more subscribers come before non-subscribers. ROC AUC is the
chance that a random subscriber is ranked above a random non-subscriber; a random ranking
gives the diagonal. `{python} percent(summary["confidence"], 0)` interval for `{python} best`: `{python} f"{low.loc['roc_auc', best]:.3f}"` to
`{python} f"{high.loc['roc_auc', best]:.3f}"`. The call centre only uses the top of the
list, which is why the business metric on the previous slides is recall in the top share.
:::

```{python}
#| label: age-setup
ages = segments[(segments["factor"] == "age_band") & (segments["version"] == best)]
ages = ages.set_index("segment")
most_called = ages["share_called"].idxmax()
least_called = ages["share_called"].idxmin()
claim(ages["share_called"].max() > 3 * ages["share_called"].min(),
      "The ranking calls the age bands at very different rates.")
claim(list(ages["share_called"].sort_values().index) == list(ages["base_rate"].sort_values().index),
      "The ranking calls the age bands in the order of their subscription rates.")
```

## `{python} best` calls `{python} percent(ages.loc[most_called, "share_called"])` of contacts aged `{python} most_called` but `{python} percent(ages.loc[least_called, "share_called"])` of those aged `{python} least_called` {#who-is-called}

```{python}
#| label: age-figure
#| fig-cap: "Test contacts by age band: the share called, and the share who subscribed."
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bar chart with two bars per age band: the share of the band that is called and the band's subscription rate. The bands are called in the same order as their subscription rates; the oldest band is called far more often than the others."
claim(most_called == ages.index[-1], "The oldest band is called most often (alt text).")
claim(ages["share_called"].max() > 2 * ages["share_called"].drop(most_called).max(),
      "The oldest band is called far more often than any other (alt text).")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.2))
rows = range(len(ages))
height = 0.38
ax.barh([r + height / 2 for r in rows], ages["share_called"], height, color=colors[best],
        label=f"Called by {best}")
ax.barh([r - height / 2 for r in rows], ages["base_rate"], height, color="#999999",
        label="Subscribed")
for r, (called, rate) in enumerate(zip(ages["share_called"], ages["base_rate"])):
    label = {"va": "center", "fontsize": 13, "zorder": 3,
             "bbox": {"facecolor": PAPER, "edgecolor": "none", "pad": 1}}
    ax.text(called + 0.005, r + height / 2, percent(called), **label)
    ax.text(rate + 0.005, r - height / 2, percent(rate), color="#555555", **label)
ax.axvline(top_share, color=INK, linestyle=":", linewidth=1.2, zorder=1)
ax.text(top_share, -0.55, f" whole list: {percent(top_share, 0)} called",
        fontsize=13, va="bottom")
ax.set_yticks(list(rows), ages.index)
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_ylabel("Age band")
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(lambda x, _: percent(x, 0))
ax.set_xlim(0, ages[["share_called", "base_rate"]].max().max() * 1.18)
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="center right")
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
`{python} best` calls the age bands in the order of their subscription rates: it follows
the outcome. Contacts aged `{python} most_called` subscribe at
`{python} percent(ages.loc[most_called, "base_rate"])`, against
`{python} percent(ages.loc[least_called, "base_rate"])` for those aged
`{python} least_called`. Age is a model input and a protected characteristic in UK equality
law, so ordering marketing calls by it needs legal review before any UK deployment: see the
model card's ethical considerations. The smallest band has
`{python} f"{ages['n'].min():,}"` test contacts, so its estimates are the noisiest.
:::

```{python}
#| label: calibration-setup
cal = calibration[calibration["version"] == best]
gap = (cal["mean_predicted"] - cal["observed_rate"]).abs()
claim(gap.max() < 0.05, "The best release's probabilities can be read as rates.")
```

## `{python} best`'s predicted probabilities are within `{python} f"{100 * gap.max():.1f}"` points of the observed rates {#calibration}

```{python}
#| label: calibration-figure
#| fig-cap: "Calibration on the test contacts, in equal-sized bins. Points on the dashed diagonal are perfectly calibrated."
#| fig-alt: "Points joined by a line: observed subscription rate against mean predicted probability, with a dashed diagonal. The points lie close to the diagonal; most bins have low predicted probabilities and one bin is much higher."
claim((cal["mean_predicted"] < 0.25).sum() > len(cal) / 2,
      "Most bins have low predicted probabilities (alt text).")
claim(cal["mean_predicted"].max() > 2 * cal["mean_predicted"].median(),
      "One bin's predictions are much higher than the rest (alt text).")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.2))
limit = cal[["mean_predicted", "observed_rate"]].max().max() * 1.05
ax.plot([0, limit], [0, limit], linestyle="--", color="#555555", linewidth=1)
ax.plot(cal["mean_predicted"], cal["observed_rate"], marker="o", markersize=7,
        linewidth=2.5, color=colors[best], label=best)
ax.set_xlabel("Mean predicted probability")
ax.set_ylabel("Observed subscription rate")
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(lambda x, _: percent(x, 0))
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(lambda x, _: percent(x, 0))
ax.set_aspect("equal")
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Calibrated probabilities can be read as rates: of contacts given a probability near some
value, about that share subscribe. Each of the `{python} cal["bin"].nunique()` points is a
bin of about `{python} f"{cal['n'].median():,.0f}"` test contacts; the largest gap between a
bin's mean prediction and its observed rate is `{python} f"{100 * gap.max():.1f}"`
percentage points. This matters for planning: the expected number of subscribers from a
campaign is the sum of the called contacts' probabilities. The probabilities are calibrated
to this data's base rate, so a client with a different rate needs recalibration.
:::

```{python}
#| label: caveat-setup
recall = metrics[metrics["metric"] == "recall_top10"].set_index("version")
overlap = recall.loc[best, "low"] <= recall.loc[rival, "high"]
claim(overlap, "The recall intervals of the best release and the runner-up overlap.")


def interval(version: str) -> str:
    """A release's recall interval, as text."""
    return f"{percent(recall.loc[version, 'low'])} to {percent(recall.loc[version, 'high'])}"
```

## These results do not yet show how `{python} best` will do for a client {#caveats .smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- **One bank's past campaigns.** Re-evaluate on the client's own recent contacts.
- **A random split.** A split by time would show how the ranking does on future campaigns.
- **Campaign fields.** `day`, `month` and `campaign` are only known once a campaign has
  started; a ranking made before it needs a release without them.
- **A small lead.** `{python} best`'s recall interval (`{python} interval(best)`) overlaps
  `{python} rival`'s (`{python} interval(rival)`).
- **Age.** The bands are called at very different rates: legal review comes first.
:::

::: {.notes}
Each point appears on a click. The data are a Portuguese bank's phone campaigns, documented
in data/README.md. The test contacts are a random sample of all dates, so they share
seasons and conditions with the training rows; a time split is the honest test of a future
campaign. The intervals are `{python} percent(summary["confidence"], 0)` percentile intervals over
`{python} f"{summary['n_bootstrap']:,}"` paired bootstrap resamples of the test set: they
reflect test-set sampling only, not a new bank, a new year or a change in who is called.
Overlapping intervals do not mean the releases are equal, but the lead is small. The model
card lists the legal and data-protection reviews as open TODOs.
:::

```{python}
#| label: decision-setup
wins = [value.loc[m, best] == (value.loc[m].max() if higher else value.loc[m].min())
        for m, (_, higher, _) in shown.items()]
claim(all(wins), "The best release is best on every metric shown, against every release.")
```

## We decide: offer `{python} best`, after a legal review of its use of age {#decision}

- **Offer `{python} best`** for the next client campaign: it is the best release on every
  metric we report.
- **Before it runs:** the legal review of age and a data-protection review.
- **Next evaluation:** the client's own recent contacts, split by time, with a release
  that does not use the campaign fields.

::: {.notes}
The decision follows from the slides before: `{python} best` reaches the most subscribers
for the same `{python} f"{calls:,}"` calls, ranks the whole list best and gives usable
probabilities. Its lead over `{python} rival` is small, so the next evaluation, on the
client's data and split by time, decides whether the lead holds. For investors: the product
is the ranking, and each release is measured the same way, from one results file, so the
next release's deck is a re-render, not a rewrite.
:::
